raw_response:
I will keep my land in the usual Quzhou pattern: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same fields. I am assuming I have `10 mu` of cropland, because you did not give a farm size. I would not split into many crops. In Quzhou, wheat-maize rotation is still the main system, with most farmland in that pattern, and the local climate fits it: hot rainy summers, dry winters, and most irrigation pressure falls on wheat, not maize. I also do not want a management plan that is too complicated for my age. So I will plant one winter wheat crop across all 10 mu, then after harvest I will seed summer maize right into the wheat stubble. I will use good seed, but I will not chase the very highest inputs. For wheat, I will keep nitrogen moderate, add enough phosphorus and potassium to stay balanced, irrigate twice, and control disease and aphids with two pesticide passes if needed. For maize, I will use a hybrid, keep one timely irrigation as backup because summer rain usually carries most of the crop here, and I will use one or two pesticide sprays depending on pressure, mainly for armyworm, corn borer, and leaf disease. I will plough before wheat to loosen the soil and help root growth, then use no-tillage for maize so I can sow fast after wheat harvest and save labor. This is the plan I would actually choose because it matches Quzhou practice, saves water, keeps labor manageable, and still gives me a solid grain harvest. I’m basing this on local Quzhou and Hebei sources showing Quzhou is dominated by wheat-maize rotation, with recent Quzhou demonstration yields around `725 kg/mu` wheat and `797 kg/mu` maize at moderate nitrogen rates, plus Ministry of Agriculture fertilizer guidance for south-central Hebei winter wheat: https://www.moa.gov.cn/xw/qg/202107/t20210720_6372348.htm , https://qzsyz.cau.edu.cn/art/2024/10/8/art_46317_1039835.html , https://www.moa.gov.cn/xw/zxfb/202209/t20220922_6411293.htm , https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5290742/
